threads_text: Cloudflare says its hosted GLM-5.3 model sent 155 answers that contained data from other customers' requests over almost two weeks. A cache that was too small plus an engine bug let very long prompts read leftovers from earlier ones. Would you still send private data to a cloud AI model?
caption:
Cloudflare says its hosted GLM-5.3 AI model returned data from other customers' requests in 155 responses between August 27 and September 9.
A cache that was too small and a bug in the SGLang engine let very long prompts read leftovers from earlier requests.
An outside researcher reported it, and Cloudflare fixed it within a day.

Would you trust a cloud AI with your company's data?

site_article.headline: Cloudflare says GLM-5.3 bug exposed customer data in 155 responses
site_article.dek: An undersized cache and an inference engine bug let very long prompts on Workers AI read data left over from other requests.
site_article.summary: Cloudflare disclosed on October 26, 2026, that its hosted GLM-5.3 model on Workers AI returned data from other customers' requests in 155 responses. The exposure ran from August 27 to September 9, 2026, and Cloudflare said it found no evidence of deliberate exploitation.
site_article.seo_title: Cloudflare GLM-5.3 bug exposed data in 155 Workers AI replies
site_article.seo_description: Cloudflare says a cache misconfiguration and an SGLang bug let its GLM-5.3 model return other customers' data in 155 responses before a September fix.
site_article.answer_summary: Cloudflare says its GLM-5.3 model on Workers AI returned other customers' data in 155 responses between August 27 and September 9, 2026, because of an undersized cache and an SGLang bug.

paragraphs.text: Cloudflare disclosed on October 26, 2026, that the GLM-5.3 model it hosts on its Workers AI service returned data from other customers' requests in 155 responses, according to Unite.AI and Data Studios. The exposure began on August 27, 2026, when the model launched on the platform, and ended with a fix on September 9.

Every affected response came from a prompt longer than 681,280 tokens. Cloudflare said a small number of customers received such responses but did not give an exact count, Data Studios reported. The company also did not describe what kind of data appeared in the responses or how affected customers were notified.

Cloudflare traced the problem to two faults that combined, according to Unite.AI. GLM-5.3 was deployed with a context window of 1,048,576 tokens, but the memory pool that holds the model's key value cache during the prefill stage could store only 681,280 tokens.

The second fault was a bug in SGLang, the open source inference engine Cloudflare uses, when it runs prefill and decode on separate machines. Requests that were too long for the cache were swapped for a placeholder instead of being rejected, and the decode stage then read stale cache pages left behind by earlier requests. Clients received a normal success code rather than an error, so nothing signaled a problem.
How it was found and fixed

Security researcher Gadi Evron of Knostic reported the issue through Cloudflare's HackerOne bug bounty program on September 8, 2026. Cloudflare declared an incident on September 9, set the model to private about 40 minutes later and restored it that evening after correcting the configuration and patching the engine, according to Data Studios and 1023 Jack.

Cloudflare raised the cache pool to about 2.04 million tokens and added a check that rejects oversized requests at admission. It proposed the engine fix to the SGLang project, which shipped it in version 0.5.20, with follow up changes in versions 0.5.21 and 0.5.22. Cloudflare recommends that other operators run version 0.5.22 or later, Unite.AI reported.

Cloudflare said it found no evidence of deliberate exploitation, based on its review of traffic patterns, and that its earlier testing had checked response codes and speed but not whether the model's output was coherent. The company now compares cache pool size with context length before any change of this kind ships. Mallory reported that Cloudflare said no other Workers AI models were affected.

The incident shows how the push for million token context windows adds new places for isolation to fail. The flaw was not in the model itself but in the serving setup around it, which customers of hosted AI services cannot inspect.

Companies running their own SGLang deployments with split prefill and decode should check their engine version and cache settings, and Evron's own report, which has not yet been published, may add detail on how the flaw was found.
